title: Saturn Devouring His Son: The True Alchemical Curse
question: Have you seen this in the Prado?
facts: Francisco Goya painted Saturn Devouring His Son directly onto the plaster dining room wall of the Quinta del Sordo between 1819 and 1823.
The work was never titled or explained by Goya; Antonio Brugada cataloged it in 1828 after Goya's death.
In alchemical treatise Atalanta Fugiens (1617) by Michael Maier, Saturn eating his child signifies lead consuming volatile matter.
Baron Frederic Emile d'Erlanger funded the transfer of the mural to canvas in 1874 before donating it to the Prado.
Neoplatonist Proclus wrote that Cronus consumes his offspring to symbolize the inexorable devourer of temporal existence.

slides.text: Baron Frederic Emile d'Erlanger funded the perilous transfer of the decaying mural from crumbling plaster to canvas in 1874.
The transferred mural was eventually donated to the Museo del Prado, where it now hangs under climate-controlled glass in Madrid.
Goya's dark vision merges classical mythology with hidden alchemical truths, surviving only because it was torn from a dying wall.

caption: Goya never intended this painting for public eyes. Painted in the absolute isolation of the Quinta del Sordo, these black murals laid bare a terrifying descent into age, madness, and alchemical ruin. Long before it became a modern internet fixture, the image mapped the heavy, consuming weight of Saturnian lead. Neoplatonists saw it as time eating its own creations; alchemists saw the dissolution of matter. Stripped from the plaster in 1874, it remains a monument to forbidden psychological depths.
